title: Code Review Guidelines
author: Sasha Petrov
body:
These guidelines describe how we review code at aliM. They apply to all production repositories.

Reviewer expectations
- Acknowledge a review request within one business day. If you cannot review in two days, decline so the author can find another reviewer.
- Read the change in full before commenting. Avoid drive-by nits without engaging with the design.
- Distinguish blocking comments from suggestions. Prefix non-blocking feedback with `nit:` or `suggestion:`.
- Approve only when you would be comfortable being paged for the change.

Author expectations
- Keep PRs under 400 lines of diff where possible. Larger changes need a design note linked from the description.
- Self-review before requesting reviewers. Address linter warnings, dead code, and obvious test gaps.
- Reply to every blocking comment, either with a code change or a written rationale.
- Squash before merge. The merge commit message is the source of truth for the change log.

Mandatory review pairs
- Inference path changes: at least one Inference team reviewer.
- Auth, IAM, or audit-log changes: at least one Security team reviewer.
- Schema migrations: at least one Platform team reviewer plus the data owner.

See RFC-0014 for the rationale behind the mandatory pairs and the escalation path when reviewers are unavailable.

title: Compensation Philosophy
author: Priya Shah
body:
aliM AI Institute compensates employees based on level, performance, and market. Our philosophy is summarized below.

1. Pay at or above market. We target the 65th percentile of comparable AI labs and tech companies for base salary, and the 75th percentile for total compensation including equity, in our primary geographies (Montreal, San Francisco).

2. Bands, not negotiation. Every role is mapped to a level and every level has a published internal band. We do not negotiate against the band; we offer the right point of the band based on experience and demonstrated impact.

3. Annual cycle. Comp adjustments happen in February each year, based on the H2 review of the previous year. Off-cycle adjustments require VP approval and are reserved for promotions and material role changes.

4. Equity refresh. Annual refresh grants are issued in February for employees with at least 12 months of tenure, sized to maintain target equity value.

5. Geographic differential. SF compensation is 1.15x of Montreal compensation at the same level for base salary. Equity grants are uniform globally.

Comp bands themselves are confidential and held by People Operations. For questions about your individual compensation, contact your manager or Wei Zhao (wei.zhao@alim.example).

title: Performance Review Framework
author: Priya Shah
body:
Reviews happen twice a year.

- H1 review: July, covering January through June.
- H2 review: January, covering July through December.

Each cycle includes:

1. Self-review (2 weeks). Reflect on goals, impact, growth areas.
2. Manager review (2 weeks). Draft rating and written feedback.
3. Peer feedback (2 weeks, parallel). 3-5 peers nominated by the reviewee and manager.
4. Calibration meeting (1 day). Managers across a function calibrate ratings to ensure consistency.
5. Skip-level and HR review.
6. Delivery (1 week). Manager delivers in 1:1.

Ratings (5-point scale):
- Needs Improvement
- Meets Expectations
- Strong Performance
- Exceeds Expectations
- Outstanding

Promotions are decided in the H2 cycle. Promotion requires sustained Exceeds or Outstanding ratings at level, plus manager, skip-level, and HR endorsement.

Performance Improvement Plans (PIPs) are not part of the review cycle. They may be initiated off-cycle when sustained performance concerns are documented.

title: Architecture Overview - Inference Stack
author: Kenji Watanabe
body:
The aliM inference stack serves customer-facing model traffic for the Applied product. This document describes the high-level architecture as of March 2026.

Components

1. Edge ingress (Cloudflare) terminates TLS and provides DDoS protection.
2. API Gateway (in-house, Go) handles authentication, request validation, rate limiting, and per-tenant routing.
3. Inference Service (Python, Triton backend) serves model traffic against the GPU pool. Currently 12 A100-80G GPUs, scaling to 32 H100s by end of Q2 with the cluster migration (see RFC-0023).
4. Cache layer (Redis Enterprise) caches deterministic prompt outputs and embedding vectors.
5. Vector store (Qdrant) holds embeddings for retrieval-augmented endpoints.
6. Observability: OpenTelemetry traces, Prometheus metrics, Loki logs. Dashboards in Grafana.

Request flow
Client -> Cloudflare -> API Gateway -> Inference Service -> (optionally Vector store -> back to inference) -> Client.

SLOs
- Availability: 99.9% monthly.
- p99 latency (non-streaming): under 400 ms at 80th-percentile workload.
- p99 latency (streaming first-token): under 250 ms.

On-call
Platform Engineering owns the inference stack on-call rotation. SRE (Jamal Greene) owns the rotation tooling.

Open work
- Cluster migration to H100 (RFC-0023, in progress).
- Multi-region active-active (RFC-0047, decision pending).
- Cost reductions on the cache layer (see Q1 2026 cost retro).

title: RFC-0023: Migration to H100 Cluster
author: Alice Chen
body:
Status: Accepted, in progress
Authors: Alice Chen, Sasha Petrov
Reviewers: Marcus Liu, Kenji Watanabe, Hina Rahimi, Dana Okafor

Summary
Migrate the inference cluster from A100-80G to H100 GPUs, increase the pool from 12 to 32 GPUs, and adopt TensorRT-LLM as the default backend for the Applied inference path.

Motivation
Current p99 latency at 80th-percentile workload is 290 ms; the target for the Q2 Applied launch is 180 ms. Internal benchmarks indicate H100 with TensorRT-LLM reduces p99 by 38-45% at our shape distribution. Cost per 1k tokens is projected to drop 22% net of capital depreciation.

Plan
Phase 1 (Q1 2026): provision 16 H100s alongside the existing A100 pool. Mirror 5% of production traffic to validate parity.
Phase 2 (early Q2): shift 50% of inference traffic to H100. Decommission 4 A100s.
Phase 3 (Q2): full cutover to H100, decommission remaining A100 pool. Reduce inference capex.

Risks
- Backend regression on long-context inputs: mitigated by canary at 5% with automated rollback.
- Vendor lock-in to TensorRT-LLM: assessed acceptable; abstraction layer planned in Q3.
- Capacity planning during cutover: Sasha owns the capacity model; reviewed weekly.

Decision: approved by Marcus Liu, October 22, 2025.

title: RFC-0031: Vector Database Selection
author: Kenji Watanabe
body:
Status: Accepted
Author: Kenji Watanabe
Reviewers: Sasha Petrov, Alice Chen, Hina Rahimi

Summary
Select Qdrant as the primary vector store for retrieval-augmented endpoints. Replaces the prior pgvector-on-Postgres setup, which has reached scale ceiling for our embedding volume.

Options considered
- pgvector (current): operationally familiar, but recall and latency degrade past ~50M vectors and we are projected to exceed 200M by Q3.
- Pinecone: managed, low operational burden; ruled out for data residency (must run in Canadian region) and cost at our projected scale.
- Weaviate: capable, but the operational story for our scale was weaker in our benchmarks.
- Qdrant (selected): strong recall on HNSW with quantization; supports hybrid sparse/dense; self-hostable in our Quebec region; clear scaling story.

Decision
Adopt Qdrant. Operate self-hosted on the Montreal cluster. Migrate pgvector workloads on a per-collection basis through Q4 2025. Maintain pgvector as a fallback for one quarter post-migration before deprecating.

Operational
Backups: nightly snapshots to encrypted S3-compatible storage.
Capacity: start with 6 nodes; alert at 70% memory or 80% disk.
Security: see DOC-0078 (vendor security review) and the threat model for the inference service.

Decision: approved by Sasha Petrov, September 18, 2025.

title: Runbook - Inference SLO Degradation
author: Jamal Greene
body:
Trigger
PagerDuty alert: inference-p99-latency-high. Alert fires when p99 latency on the Applied inference path exceeds 600 ms for 5 consecutive minutes.

Severity
- SEV-2 by default. Promote to SEV-1 if customer-impacting error rate > 1% sustained.

Step 1: Acknowledge and assess (within 5 minutes)
- Open the Grafana dashboard `inf-overview`. Confirm latency band and which GPU pool is hot.
- Confirm whether the alert correlates with a deploy in the last 60 minutes. If yes, jump to Step 4 (rollback).

Step 2: Check the obvious
- Cache hit rate (Redis dashboard). A sudden drop indicates either a cache flush event or an upstream change.
- Queue depth on the inference workers. Sustained queue depth > 30 indicates capacity exhaustion.
- GPU utilization. Sustained > 95% means we are out of headroom.

Step 3: Shed load (if needed)
- Engage the gateway rate limiter for non-priority tenants. Command: `aliMctl gateway throttle --tier=free --limit=50%`.
- Notify SRE channel and link the incident to the rate-limiting action.

Step 4: Rollback (if recent deploy)
- Use `aliMctl deploy rollback inference --to=previous`. This is safe; canary is preserved.

Step 5: Escalation
- If not resolved within 20 minutes, page Sasha Petrov (Platform on-call backup) and Kenji Watanabe (inference owner).
- If customer-impacting > 30 minutes, page Marcus Liu (CTO).

Post-incident
- Open a postmortem ticket within 24 hours regardless of severity. Use the postmortem template.

title: Runbook - Training Cluster Outage
author: Diego Alvarez
body:
Trigger
Slack alert from `#alerts-training`: one of: cluster control-plane unreachable, NCCL collective failure rate > 5% for 10 minutes, or scheduler refusing job submissions.

Severity
- SEV-3 unless an active training run is blocked. Promote to SEV-2 if a research milestone is at risk.

Diagnostic checklist
1. Confirm the cluster is reachable: `kubectl get nodes` from the bastion. If unreachable, escalate to networking on-call (Diego or Sasha).
2. Check NCCL diagnostics. Run `aliMctl train nccl-check` from any node. NCCL collective failures are usually traceable to NVLink or InfiniBand faults.
3. Check the scheduler logs in Loki. Job submissions can be refused if the scheduler queue is saturated.
4. Check storage: training jobs pull from the shared filesystem; a storage stall manifests as job-level hangs.

Common fixes
- NCCL collective failure due to a bad GPU: cordon the node, drain the workload, file a hardware ticket.
- Scheduler queue saturation: pause low-priority eval jobs to free the queue.
- Storage stall: page the storage on-call.

Escalation
- 30 minutes unresolved: page Sasha (Platform).
- 1 hour unresolved with research blocked: page Hina (Research).

title: Postmortem - May 2025 Inference Outage
author: Sasha Petrov
body:
Incident: aliM-INC-2025-014
Severity: SEV-1
Date: May 14, 2025
Duration: 02:18-04:47 UTC (2 hours 29 minutes)
Customer impact: ~62% of inference requests on the Applied path returned 5xx during the window. Customer-impacting minutes: 149.

Summary
A deploy of the inference service introduced a regression in the request-batching logic. Under load, batches of long-context requests exceeded the GPU memory budget, causing CUDA OOMs that cascaded into worker crashes. The pod restart loop saturated the cluster autoscaler, preventing healthy capacity from coming online.

Timeline (UTC)
- 02:18 - Deploy `inference-srv@2a4f1c0` rolled out. Canary at 5% appeared healthy.
- 02:24 - Canary expanded to 25%. Latency p99 climbed but stayed under alert threshold.
- 02:34 - Full rollout. Alert `inference-p99-latency-high` fired.
- 02:36 - On-call (Kenji Watanabe) acknowledged.
- 02:48 - On-call attempted rollback. Rollback succeeded for new pods but existing pods continued to crash and restart.
- 03:15 - Sasha Petrov paged. Identified the crash loop blocking autoscaler recovery.
- 03:30 - Manually evicted all inference pods and cordoned the cluster for 10 minutes to break the loop.
- 03:45 - Cluster recovered. New pods on previous-known-good image came online.
- 04:47 - All SLOs back to baseline. Incident closed.

Root cause
The batching change increased the upper bound of the per-batch memory footprint. The change passed staging tests but staging traffic did not include the long-context shape that surfaced the issue. The canary metrics did not capture memory-pressure signals, only latency.

Contributing factors
- Canary metrics did not include CUDA memory pressure or OOM rate.
- The rollback path did not handle in-flight crashing pods cleanly.
- No production traffic-shape diversity in staging.

Action items
- AI-001 (Kenji): add CUDA memory pressure and OOM rate to canary signal. Done June 4, 2025.
- AI-002 (Diego): add forced-eviction step to the rollback playbook. Done June 12, 2025.
- AI-003 (Sasha): introduce production-shape replay into staging. Tracked through Q3 2025.
- AI-004 (Jamal): tune the inference autoscaler to prefer eviction over scale-up when crash-loop is detected. Done June 28, 2025.

Internal contact for follow-up: sasha.petrov@alim.example.

title: Code Style Guide - Python
author: Alice Chen
body:
aliM Python style guide. Applies to all production Python code; research notebooks are exempted except where promoted to production.

Formatting and linting
- Formatter: `ruff format`. Line length 100.
- Linter: `ruff` with the project ruleset. CI fails on lint errors.
- Type checker: `mypy --strict` for production packages; `mypy` (non-strict) for tooling.

Project layout
- Source under `src/`, tests under `tests/`. Test files mirror the source structure.
- One package per service; shared utilities live in `aliM-common`.

Logging
- Use `structlog` with JSON output in production. Plain console in development.
- Never log secrets, full PII, or full prompt content. Mask values with `aliM_common.logging.mask`.

Errors
- Raise typed exceptions defined in the service-level `errors.py`. Never raise bare `Exception`.
- Wrap external library errors at the boundary.

Testing
- Pytest. One assertion concept per test.
- Coverage target: 80% on changed code, enforced in CI for new packages.

Code review
- Approvals required: one for routine changes, two for cross-service changes, plus a security review for anything touching auth, secrets, or PII handling.

author: Maya Patel
body:
aliM TypeScript style guide. Applies to all frontend code and Node-based services.

Tooling
- Formatter: Prettier. Line length 100.
- Linter: ESLint with the aliM ruleset (extends `airbnb-typescript`, plus our security rules).
- Type checking: TypeScript strict mode. No `any` in production code; `unknown` is allowed at boundaries.

title: API Spec - Inference Service v2
author: Kenji Watanabe
body:
Service: Inference v2 (`/v2/infer`)
Status: GA since January 15, 2026. v1 deprecated, supported through June 30, 2026.

Authentication
- Bearer token in `Authorization` header. Tokens are tenant-scoped.
- Service-to-service calls additionally include the `X-aliM-Caller` header.

Endpoints
- POST `/v2/infer` - synchronous completion or streaming when `stream=true`.
- POST `/v2/infer/batch` - asynchronous batch submission, polled via `/v2/infer/batch/{id}`.

Request schema (sync)
Required: `model`, `messages` (array of role/content).
Optional: `temperature`, `top_p`, `max_tokens`, `stream`, `tools`, `tool_choice`.
Maximum input tokens: 128,000. Maximum output tokens: 16,000.

Response schema
`id`, `model`, `choices[]` (each with `message` and `finish_reason`), `usage` (input_tokens, output_tokens).

Error model
Standard 4xx/5xx HTTP. Errors include `code` (machine-readable), `message`, and `request_id`.

Rate limits
- Per-tenant. Default 10,000 requests per minute, 1,000,000 input tokens per minute.
- 429 returned with `Retry-After` header.

Observability
Every request emits a span with tenant, model, prompt tokens, completion tokens, and latency, but never the prompt or completion content.

title: API Spec - Document Ingestion Service
author: Alice Chen
body:
Service: Document Ingestion (`/v1/docs`)
Status: Beta. GA target Q3 2026.

Purpose
Accepts customer documents for indexing into the customer's tenant-isolated knowledge store. Documents are chunked, embedded, and stored in Qdrant with tenant-scoped indices.

Authentication
- Bearer token, tenant-scoped (same scheme as inference).

Endpoints
- POST `/v1/docs` - submit a document for ingestion. Supports JSON metadata + content body.
- DELETE `/v1/docs/{id}` - delete a document and remove its embeddings.
- GET `/v1/docs/{id}` - retrieve metadata and content (content returns redacted view based on caller).

Content handling
- PII detection runs synchronously at ingest. Detected PII is annotated in metadata; redaction policy is per-tenant.
- Embedding model: `aliM-embed-v3` (768-dim). Embeddings are stored alongside the source chunk in Qdrant.
- Document size limit: 10 MB. Chunk size: 800 tokens with 100-token overlap.

Tenant isolation
- Indices are namespaced per tenant. Cross-tenant retrieval is impossible at the storage layer; enforcement is also redundant at the application layer.

Auditing
- Every ingest, retrieval, and delete is logged. See the data classification policy for retention.

title: RFC-0044: Knowledge Assistant Permission Model
author: Alice Chen
body:
Status: Draft
Authors: Alice Chen, Dana Okafor
Reviewers: Marcus Liu, Sasha Petrov, Priya Shah, Tomas Ferreira

Summary
Define the permission model for the internal Knowledge Assistant prototype. Roles, sensitivities, audiences, and PII categories combine to determine what content is retrievable, what is presented in answers, and what is logged.

Roles
Baseline: `employee`. Function-specific elevated roles: `hr`, `engineering`, `security`. A user holds at most one functional role plus the baseline.

Document signals (corpus schema)
- `sensitivity`: public | internal | confidential | restricted.
- `intended_audience`: the author's stated readership. Values: company-wide, people-ops, engineering, security, engineering-and-security, people-ops-and-security, function-leads.
- `department`: the team that produced the document.

`intended_audience` is the author's signal, not a permission list. Mapping audience to effective access for each role is the work of this RFC.

Audience to role mapping (proposed)
- `company-wide`: all roles can retrieve.
- `people-ops`: hr only.
- `engineering`: engineering and security.
- `security`: security only.
- `engineering-and-security`: engineering and security.
- `people-ops-and-security`: hr and security.
- `function-leads`: hr, engineering, and security (excludes baseline `employee`).

Sensitivity overlay
- `public` / `internal`: retrievable by any user whose role is in the audience mapping above.
- `confidential`: additionally requires an elevated functional role (`hr`, `engineering`, or `security`).
- `restricted`: additionally limited to `hr` or `security`.

PII handling at retrieval and generation
- PII categories: `name`, `contact`, `identifier`, `financial`, `sensitive_narrative` (see the data dictionary for definitions).
- Detection runs at ingest and again at generation time. Ground-truth labels in `pii_labels.jsonl` are used for offline evaluation only and are not consumed at runtime.
- For roles other than `hr`, the categories `identifier`, `financial`, and `sensitive_narrative` are masked even when the document is otherwise readable.
- `name` is not masked. `contact` is masked when the value is identifiably personal (personal phones, home addresses); work emails are emitted unmodified.

Auditing
- Every retrieval logs: caller, document ids considered, document ids included in the answer, redactions applied, and refusal reason if any.
- Logs are tamper-evident (signed batches) and retained per the records retention schedule.

Open questions
- How do we handle indirect prompt injection that originates inside a document the user is permitted to read?
- How do we behave when the answer would require combining accessible and inaccessible documents?
- Should we expose a 'refused content existed' signal to the user without revealing what was refused?

title: RFC-0052: Observability Stack Consolidation
author: Jamal Greene
body:
Status: Accepted
Author: Jamal Greene
Reviewers: Sasha Petrov, Diego Alvarez, Dana Okafor

Summary
Consolidate metrics, logs, and traces onto a single OpenTelemetry-based pipeline. Phase out the legacy Statsd-based metrics pipeline by end of Q3 2026.

Motivation
Two pipelines mean two outages to debug, double the SDK surface area, and inconsistent tagging across services.

- Phase 3: Statsd pipeline decommissioned. Cost savings approximately 18,000 USD per month.

- Tag-rename churn for dashboards: mitigated by a rename map and gradual cutover.
- Sampling differences: documented in the migration guide.

Decision: approved by Sasha Petrov, February 12, 2026.

title: Architecture - Training Data Pipeline
author: Lea Dubois
body:
The training data pipeline ingests source datasets, applies safety and quality filters, formats them for training, and produces sharded training corpora consumed by the training cluster.

Stages
1. Ingest: source datasets land in tenant-scoped S3-compatible storage. Provenance metadata is recorded on each blob.
2. License gate: any source without a license declaration is quarantined and reviewed manually.
3. Deduplication: cross-source dedup at the document and near-duplicate (MinHash) level.
4. PII filtering: a multi-detector pipeline removes documents with high-density PII, masks low-density occurrences.
5. Safety filtering: removes documents matching the safety policy (CSAM, doxxing, etc.). Logs blocked sources for review.
6. Format: tokenize and pack into training shards.
7. Hash-pin: every shard is content-hashed and pinned. Training runs reference shards by hash.

Access
- Source ingestion is logged and limited to research engineers.
- Read access to the filtered corpus is limited to the training cluster service account and a small group of research engineers.
- The PII filter and safety filter logs are reviewed monthly by Dana Okafor and Hina Rahimi.

Out of scope here
- Customer ingestion (covered separately in the document ingestion service spec).
- Evaluation datasets (managed by the research team).

title: RFC-0047: Multi-Region Active-Active
author: Sasha Petrov

Summary
Add a second active region (initial choice: US-East) to serve U.S. customers with lower latency and to provide failover for the Montreal primary.

title: Postmortem - Data Pipeline Backfill, February 2026
author: Lea Dubois
body:
Incident: aliM-INC-2026-009
Severity: SEV-3
Date: February 22, 2026
Duration: 12 hours of incorrect data in the safety eval corpus
Customer impact: none. Internal evaluation regression caused by the issue was contained.

Summary
A change to the safety filter introduced an off-by-one in the chunk-boundary handling. Documents larger than 800 tokens were truncated mid-token, producing malformed entries. The filter ran cleanly without erroring, so the issue was not detected until the next-day eval review flagged a regression.

Timeline
- Feb 21 16:00 - filter change merged and deployed.
- Feb 22 00:00 - nightly pipeline ran with the bug. Affected 1.2M documents (~3% of the corpus).
- Feb 22 12:30 - Hina noticed eval regression and traced it to the safety corpus.
- Feb 23 09:00 - bug identified, fix merged, backfill scheduled.

Root cause
Boundary check used `<` instead of `<=` when slicing on chunk boundaries.

Action items
- AI-001 (Lea): add corpus health metrics to the eval review.
- AI-002 (Lea): add a property-based test for chunk-boundary handling.
- AI-003 (Sasha): add a 'sanity-eval' canary that runs on every data pipeline change before the corpus is consumed downstream.

title: Architecture - Authentication and Authorization
author: Dana Okafor
body:
Authentication
- Customer-facing: OIDC against the tenant's IdP, brokered through our auth gateway. Tokens are short-lived (15 minutes), refreshed via the refresh token flow.
- Service-to-service: mTLS with SPIFFE identities. No long-lived secrets in services.
- Internal: SSO via Okta, hardware second factor required, session length 8 hours.

Authorization
- Customer API: tenant + role + scope. Role is asserted in the OIDC claims; scope is per-API.
- Service-to-service: callers are identified by SPIFFE ID. Authz checked at the API gateway and re-checked at the service boundary.
- Internal tooling: Okta groups drive RBAC in each tool.

Sensitive operations
- Deploy to production: requires PR approval + Okta MFA challenge at the deploy time.
- Access to HRIS, payroll, or security incident systems: separate Okta groups, just-in-time approval via Tomas (HR) or Dana (Security).

Secrets
- All secrets in Vault. Service tokens fetched at startup, refreshed periodically.
- No secrets in environment variables in production.

Known gaps
- The Knowledge Assistant prototype is not yet wired into Okta for end-user auth; it currently consumes a role claim header. This is acceptable for the prototype phase only. See RFC-0044.

title: Data Classification Policy
author: Dana Okafor
body:
All aliM data is classified into one of four levels. Classification drives storage, access, retention, and disposal.

Public
- Anything we publish externally (marketing, blog, open-source code, public papers).
- May be replicated freely.

Internal
- General company information not for external sharing (handbook, all-hands recaps, team pages).
- Accessible to all employees. Not shared externally without approval.

Confidential
- Information that would cause harm if leaked: financial records, security incident details, compensation data, customer contracts, research roadmaps.
- Access on a need-to-know basis. Auditable. Encryption at rest and in transit required.

Restricted
- Information that would cause severe harm if leaked: payroll detail, HRIS extracts, active investigations, source-code keys, PII at scale.
- Highly scoped access. JIT approvals. Hardware MFA required. All access is logged and reviewed.

Defaults
- Anything not classified is treated as Confidential by default until classified explicitly.
- Customer data inherits the customer's contractual classification.

Retention
- Public: indefinite.
- Internal: 7 years.
- Confidential: 7 years unless contractually required longer.
- Restricted: minimum needed for the lawful or business purpose; reviewed annually.

Owner: CISO (Dana Okafor). Reviewed annually.

title: Penetration Test Report - Q2 2026 (Summary)
author: Reza Kahn
body:
Test conducted by NorthSec Consulting between March 30 and April 17, 2026. Scope: customer-facing inference API, document ingestion API, internal Knowledge Assistant prototype.

Findings (10 total): 1 high, 3 medium, 6 low. None critical.

High
- F-2026-04-H1: SSRF via the document ingestion `url` field. Authenticated users could submit URLs that the ingestion service resolved server-side, including internal metadata endpoints. CWE-918. Remediation: deny-list of RFC 1918 + cloud metadata IPs at the resolver, plus an allow-list of public schemes. Status: shipped April 21 (Diego). Verified by NorthSec.

- F-2026-04-M1: Insufficient rate limiting on tenant token refresh. Could enable account-takeover via brute force. CWE-307. Remediation in progress; Reza tracking through Q2.
- F-2026-04-M2: Verbose error messages on the Knowledge Assistant prototype leak internal stack frames. CWE-209. Remediation: error sanitization layer. Owner: Alice. Target May 8.
- F-2026-04-M3: CSRF protection missing on three internal tools. Owner: Maya. Target April 30.

Six low findings related to security headers, CSP refinements, dependency hygiene, and logging coverage. Tracked in the security backlog.

title: Vulnerability Disclosure - Credential Stuffing Attempt, Q1 2026

title: Threat Model - Inference Service
author: Dana Okafor
body:
Asset: customer-facing inference service.
Trust boundaries: edge ingress, API gateway, inference workers, vector store, model artifacts.

Threats considered
1. Credential compromise of a tenant API key. Mitigated by short-lived tokens, IP allow-listing for enterprise tenants, and anomaly detection on usage patterns.
2. Cross-tenant data leakage at the storage layer. Mitigated by per-tenant index namespacing in Qdrant and tenant-scoped database connections. Verified by NorthSec pentest Q2 2026.
3. Prompt injection from user input causing the model to expose system prompts. Mitigated by input/output filters and minimal system-prompt content. Residual risk: accepted; tracked.
4. Model weight exfiltration via inference API queries (extraction attacks). Mitigated by rate limiting and response watermarking research; residual risk: documented and accepted for the current product stage.
5. Denial-of-service via expensive long-context queries. Mitigated by per-tenant token-rate limits and cost-based throttling.
6. Compromise of a GPU node. Mitigated by short-lived node identities, vault-issued credentials at boot, and node-level isolation.
7. Tampering with model artifacts in storage. Mitigated by content hashing and signed artifact pinning.

Open
- Indirect prompt injection from retrieved documents in RAG flows (covered separately in DOC-0074).

Reviewed by Sasha Petrov (engineering), Marcus Liu (CTO). Next review: Q3 2026.

title: Threat Model - Knowledge Assistant Prototype
author: Dana Okafor
body:
Asset: internal Knowledge Assistant prototype (RAG over the internal corpus, role-aware).
Trust boundaries: identity provider, application service, retrieval layer, LLM provider.

Threats considered
1. Authorization bypass at retrieval. A user retrieves content their role should not have access to. Mitigated by enforcing role + sensitivity at the retrieval layer. Status: addressed; verified by integration tests.
2. Authorization bypass at generation. Retrieved content is permitted, but generation reveals PII or sensitive fields the user should not see. Mitigated by per-role field-level masking in the answer-construction step. Status: partially addressed; PII categories covered, but free-form leakage residual.
3. Indirect prompt injection from a retrieved document. A document contains instructions to ignore prior policy, leak other documents, or change behavior. Mitigated by content sandboxing (system vs. retrieved-context separation), instruction stripping heuristics, and an output classifier that refuses if the response deviates from grounded answers. Status: partially addressed; depth of defense is the open work.
4. Inferred-information leakage. Even with redaction, an answer may reveal sensitive information through synthesis. Mitigated by topic-level guardrails for sensitive categories. Status: deferred to Q3 2026.
5. Role-elevation via document content. A document claims the reader is authorized for restricted content. Mitigated by treating role assertions as untrusted unless from the identity provider. Status: addressed.
6. Audit gap. A bad answer is given but cannot be reconstructed. Mitigated by structured logging of caller, retrieved doc ids, redactions, and grounding context. Status: addressed.
7. PII detection bypass via formatting tricks (zero-width characters, base64). Mitigated by canonicalization before detection. Status: partially addressed.
8. Tenant-isolation drift if the assistant is later extended to multi-tenant. Mitigated by per-tenant index design baked in now. Status: addressed.

Authors: Dana Okafor and Alice Chen. Reviewed: Marcus Liu, Sasha Petrov.

title: Privacy Impact Assessment - Knowledge Assistant Prototype
author: Dana Okafor
body:
Project: internal Knowledge Assistant prototype.
Authors: Dana Okafor, Alice Chen, Priya Shah.
Stage: prototype. Not in scope for customer-facing deployment.

Personal data processed
- Internal employee data: names, work emails, role, manager, department.
- Incidental data inside corpus documents: home addresses, personal phones, dates of birth, salary, performance evaluations, health-related notes for accommodations.

Purposes
- Answer employee questions about internal policies and information.
- Demonstrate access control and PII handling for the Series C diligence.

Lawful basis
- Legitimate interest (employment context); employees are informed via the IT acceptable use policy and the upcoming knowledge assistant rollout note.

Data minimization
- Corpus is intentionally tightly scoped. Restricted HR documents are excluded by default and only reachable by HR via the role-mapped retrieval.
- Generation enforces field-level masking on PII for non-HR callers.

Retention
- Query logs: 90 days for operational debugging, then anonymized.
- Audit logs: 7 years to support investigations.

Risks and mitigations
- Indirect prompt injection: covered in the assistant threat model.
- Inferred-information leakage from synthesis: deferred mitigation tracked.
- Accidental over-disclosure to non-HR roles: addressed at the retrieval and generation layers.

Sign-off
Dana Okafor (CISO), Priya Shah (VP People), Marcus Liu (CTO). Approved for prototype deployment to internal staff only.

title: Customer Data Handling Standard
author: Dana Okafor
body:
All customer data must be handled per this standard. Applies to engineering, support, and any function with access to customer-derived data.

Classification
- Customer data inherits the customer's contractual classification. By default treat it as Confidential.
- Customer PII is always Restricted regardless of the contract.

Storage
- Encryption at rest required. Logs containing customer data are equally subject to encryption.
- Cross-tenant access is forbidden at every layer; tenant scoping is enforced at storage and re-enforced at the application boundary.

Access
- Production access to customer data requires JIT approval. Standing access is not permitted.
- Engineering investigations that require customer data must be ticketed, time-bounded, and reviewed by Security.

Retention and deletion
- Per the contract; default 90 days post-termination.
- Verified deletion log available to the customer on request.

Incidents
- Any incident affecting customer data follows the incident response policy. Customer notification per contractual terms; no later than 72 hours from confirmation for SEV-1.

Owner: CISO. Reviewed annually or upon material contract change.
